blocks.p: Play is a mixed state. When two (or all) primary states are active simultaneously, they create a mixed state. If you mix two primary colors, you get a secondary color, right? Red paint mixed with blue paint makes purple paint. Same with Polyvagal primary states.
Safety + Flight/Fight = Play

Play is a combination of ventral vagal safety state activation with sympathetic flight/fight. When we play, we're active, but we're safe. We're mobile and social at the same time. We use our face and voice to signal safety to the other participant(s) in the play.

My children and I love to run around chasing each other. We play fight, we wrestle, we throw things, we scream and yell. All of these are potentially danger cues in and of themselves, but when you see our faces, you'll see smiles, eye crinkles, upright eyebrows, and shared eye contact. Our ears are still tuned to human voice, so discussing the game's rules or creating new ones on the fly isn't an issue. Our voices have a lot of range, along with laughter.

Play can also involve two nervous systems sharing attention, even if the obvious social cues are missing. Two people can share in activities like working on a puzzle or competing in chess without obvious pro-social cues. They utilize shared time, turn-taking, agreed-upon rules, and social norms. These require the individuals to have enough access to their safety states to engage without defense.

Working on a project with a co-worker can be a form of play. For example, Mercedes Corona was my podcast co-host and colleague. We developed a curriculum and presented it to our school district staff colleagues. It's a lot of work, but the two of us genuinely enjoyed the shared experience and consistently provided safety cues to each other. We exchanged ideas back and forth, challenged each other, and encouraged each other. We played for all intents and purposes, even though we were working.

Play also extends into sports: a mobilized, shared activity that involves safety cues. Of course, the other team is not looking to provide safety cues. But there's a significant difference between an opposing player using intimidation and one that actually wants to hurt you. We can see intimidation, trash-talking, and overt aggression within the rules/norms of many sports. Acting within the confines of those norms doesn't trigger a distinct neuroception of danger. But acting outside of those norms can.

In American football, the defense is allowed to tackle the quarterback. If they tackle the quarterback before he throws the ball, this is called a "sack" and has no penalty. Conversely, if the defense tackles the quarterback after throwing the ball, this is not a sack and likely will result in a penalty. It's basically against the rules to tackle the quarterback after he has thrown the ball. Or touch him on the helmet. Or below the knees. Or to land on him with your body weight... let's just say there's a lot of rules in place to protect the quarterback.

Every contextual piece can be the same: the same defensive player can make the same tackle on the same quarterback in the same spot on the field. But one type of tackle is okay, and the other is not. All the players know this and agree to the rules: a sack is fine, but the penalized tackle is not.

In fact, the offensive players take this penalty very seriously; they see tackling the quarterback after he throws it as a direct insult or threat to one of their own. The offense will come to the quarterback's aid and use physical and verbal intimidation on the offending defensive player. Then, the defensive players come to the aid of their teammate, and a mob of players shove each other for a few seconds. Then it gets broken up, and normal play resumes.

So, what's happening? The offensive players neurocept the penalty as an actual danger: a direct attack on their quarterback. They lose access to their safety state, and their play becomes something else. It turns into defensive activation, resulting in yelling and shoving. Then the defensive teammates neurocept the danger from the offense, resulting in them yelling and shoving as well. Both teams lose access to their safety state.

Play needs safety state access. If the safety state is inactive, defensive activation dominates. If defensive activation dominates, defensive behaviors occur, like hitting, yelling, running away, or giving up and isolating.

Play exercises the ability to shift up and down the Polyvagal ladder while anchored in safety. We use mobility (flight/fight) when playing, like running down a soccer field or tackling in football. We may also use shutdown when immobile in hide-and-seek or even freeze in freeze tag. Because of the safety anchoring, we can move freely up and down the ladder, building our ability to handle these shifts. Simultaneously, we strengthen the safety state, building self-regulation.

Play is essential in children. It's not just about having fun. Play is how they build the strength of their social engagement system. Adults can also build their safety state through play. However, with children, it provides the foundation for self-regulation to build on in the future. Parents and other caretakers must allow children ample time and opportunities to play with their peers and safe others in their lives.
Play can look many different ways: dance, sports, competition, puzzles, role-playing, theater... and I'd argue even video games. But let's differentiate between in-person and isolated online gaming.

In-person video gaming can have huge social, fun, or competitive components. If you can work with a teammate in a video game, you will use strategizing and problem-solving. You need to be anchored in safety to use these cognitive skills. But you also need the competitive edge that comes from the sympathetic state. There's also opportunities for social connection, like smiling with each other between rounds. You use your voice to talk with other players, working together on a shared focus.

Are video games the same as dance or baseball? Of course not, but I think there's value to gaming, especially if that's the best option you have at your disposal. If you're a parent who can't mobilize on a sunny day due to a chronic illness, then maybe you can play video games instead. Sure, a puzzle or coloring book is also a great option. But video games are... fair game, in my opinion. (Sorry for that.)

In my home, Mario Kart is a common way for my family of four to connect through play. We soothe each others' high arousal states through social interaction, like eye contact and vocal prosody. (We also antagonize each other with taunts but stay within family and social norms.) Games like Mario Kart and Animal Crossing are ones we can play together, in the same room, exchanging safety cues.

But other games, like Fortnite, require my kids and I to separate into different rooms to play together online. Fortnite is still fun, but much more competitive than casual gaming in the same room. My kids and I can still play (in the Polyvagal sense) through Fortnite, but access to safety deteriorates compared to other games. The kids bicker over who holds what weapons or brag about who has the most eliminations.

Online gaming in isolation is different from in-person, like the Fortnite example compared to Mario Kart. The players don't see each other's faces. There is opportunity for some vocal exchange, but not much, and not necessarily, as many players don't use their mics. And because there are no visual safety cues from the other players, vocal cues such as yelling, groans, swearing, bragging, taunting, and insults are easily neurocepted as danger cues, thereby shifting the participants from play to fight.

Individuals in a defensive state may be unable to handle the sympathetic mobilization of play while also accessing their safety system. They mobilize but aren't able to contain their flight/fight behavior to use for prosocial playful interaction. You can see the problem here: this person cannot exist in their safety state, but they need to for play. Their defensive activation is out of control, but needs to be under control for play. They need both mobility and safety at the same time, but struggle to.

Have you ever heard of kids who "don't play well with others"? These are them. Their defensive state is active without the safety state, resulting in breaking norms and rules. These kids lack self-regulation and struggle to accept the social cues of play from their peers.

Kids and adults who push the limit of acceptable play will end up hurting someone. They won't feel guilt over it, either. They will blame the person or shame them. You need access to the safety state to empathize and feel sorrow for hurting another. This individual has less access to the safety state and, therefore, does not feel empathy or sorrow.

It's 2017, and I'm at my son's first soccer game: a field with 12 toddlers on it. There's a mix of nervous system states present. Many have dropped down the ladder and want their parents, refuse to go on the field, need something like a snack or water, or are getting worn out. There are parents on the field, coaches, and a couple of refs, and everyone is telling the kids what to do. It's a fairly dysregulated state of affairs.

One boy in particular is highly mobilized: on the field when he's not supposed to be, not following directives from the coach or ref, and touching the ball with his hands. He's just moving around without much safety state active. His safe and social system is not developed enough to inhibit the impulses to move. He crashes into other kids and "falls" repeatedly as well.

I witnessed one thing that might shed some light on this particular soccer player's dysregulation. At one point, the child had "fallen" down and stayed on the ground despite the game around him and the adults telling him to get up. He's not in a tantrum or a meltdown; he's just lying there. His Dad walks onto the field (for the third time) to correct his behavior. The little soccer player gets up with his arms up, waiting to be held by the Dad... but the dad spins the kid around and gives him a little push back onto the field. The Dad showed no emotion or expression, didn't say anything, and provided his son no support, encouragement, or obvious signals of safety or love.

I have no idea what home life is like. Maybe Dad is typically more supportive of his child. But this little window provides a glimpse into the possible lack of support the little soccer player gets from his Dad: the lack of emotional development, the lack of safety pathways being nurtured. At that moment, it made sense to me why the child was so dysregulated, especially in an environment surrounded by other dysregulated nervous systems, noise, heat, and eyes watching. This boy was on the field and dressed for soccer, but was he playing? Not really.

I recall another time during another soccer game (maybe the same one? I don't know) when a little girl stood frozen in the middle of the field. She didn't want to go out in the first place and resisted her Mother with a quiet protest before the game began. Her body was tense as the Mother carried her out and placed her in the middle of the field. When the initial ball was kicked and the kids started scrambling, this particular little girl just stayed in her spot, frozen in place. Her muscles were tense, her eyes were wide, and she avoided all potential eye contact. She seemed unable to hear the sounds around her. Her Mother and the coach attempted to use their vocal prosody to coax her into participating, but these attempts went nowhere.

This little girl was in a state of mobilization: evidenced by the muscle tension and shallow breathing. But she was also in a state of immobilization: evidenced by not moving. She was in a freeze state. Her body prepared to both run and shut down at the same time. Not out of excitement but out of fear. Maybe of the crowd, of failure, or immense pressure from parents. When her Mom escorted her off the field, she softened immediately in relief as her Mom held her in her lap. The girl was dressed for soccer and on the field, but was she playing? Obviously not.
Well, anything is unsafe without access to the safety state or without the ability to accept safety cues from another.

When there is danger, we use flight/fight mobility. That's what we evolved to do: survive danger through movement. Thanks to the newer social engagement system, mammals can contain or repurpose their flight/fight activation for prosocial behavior. If we didn't have a safety system, we'd all be either mobile or immobile: like lizards. The mixed state of play wouldn't exist (lizards don't play). If we access the flight/fight mobilization system to play, without safety activated along with it, we're simply left with mobilized defensive behaviors: flight/fight by itself.

The safety system needs to be active for play. If safety isn't active, it's simply not play. The result is an increased heart rate without the social engagement system necessary to regulate the flight/fight impulses.

If safety is inactive, we perceive the environment and others as threatening. Our perceptual filter of safety is gone. A person in a defensive state has lost their ability to recognize safe facial cues that are necessary during play. They're also not providing those same facial cues. This person is not using vocal prosody to suggest they're a safe mammal. They've lost the ability to use their full range of voice, signaling safety to the other parties.
We need our safety state active to repurpose flight/fight activation for social engagement. Once safety is active, we can mobilize with others without risk of dysregulated flight/fight.

We can also utilize our mobilized safety state when alone. Safety plus flight/fight without others looks like exercise or focused motivation. We mobilize to meet personal goals, like in business or fitness.

blocks.prompt: Name one instance from this past week when you felt your play mixed state active. How do you know it was play?
When was the last time you felt a sense of fun? Imagination? Connection with mobility?
Do you have easily accessible ways of playing?
Do you have easily accessible people to play with?
When you think of playing, do any emotional obstacles occur within you? How about thoughts?
When was the last time you felt motivated and focused on completing a goal? How easy is it for you to feel motivated and focused on a solo task?

q: "Polyvagal Theory focuses on specific neural exercises that provide opportunities to optimize the regulation of physiological state. According to the theory, neural exercises consisting of transitory disruptions and repairs of physiological state through social interactions employing cues of safety would promote greater resilience. Play, such as peek-a-boo, is an example of a neural exercise that parents frequently employ with their children. Play provides an example of a therapeutic model in which autonomic state is disrupted and then stabilized through the recruitment of the social engagement system." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W. (2018). Polyvagal theory: A primer. In S. W. Porges & D. Dana (Eds.), Clinical Applications of the Polyvagal Theory: The Emergence of Polyvagal-Informed Therapies (pp. 50–61). W. W. Norton & Company.

blocks.p: My translation: We can increase resilience through games that disrupt and repair social interactions.

q: "Through the metaphor of play, the social engagement system is coupled with the sympathetic nervous system. This coupling enables bodily cues of mobilization to be contained within a social setting and not to erupt into aggression. However, these eruptions or tantrums frequently occur in children and adults with behavioral problems and psychiatric disorders. Research documents a consistency of a down regulated social engagement system (e.g., lack of prosody, blunted facial expression, auditory hypersensitivities, poor eye gaze) in individuals with state regulation disorders (see Porges, 2011)." (Porges)
blocks.cite: Porges, S. W. (2018). Polyvagal theory: A primer. In S. W. Porges & D. Dana (Eds.), Clinical Applications of the Polyvagal Theory: The Emergence of Polyvagal-Informed Therapies (pp. 50–61). W. W. Norton & Company.

blocks.p: My translation: The safety state repurposes flight/fight for play when it's active. Research shows less safety activation in those with behavioral and emotional regulation difficulties.
